vocab.en: to come out, fall out (살이 빠지다 = lose weight)

grammar.explanation: Many verbs end in ~거리다, which attaches to a sound or motion word to describe something happening repeatedly or continuously, like shaking, twinkling or hesitating. They conjugate like any other verb.

examples.en: The boat keeps rocking.
Stars are twinkling in the sky.
He hesitated before answering.
My hands were sticky, so I washed them.

grammar.explanation: 자기 points back to the subject of the sentence, like "his own" or "her own", and is mostly used for third persons. 자신 means "oneself" and often appears as 자기 자신 or, for the speaker, 제 자신 / 내 자신.

examples.en: Minsu cleaned his own room.
It is important to love yourself.
I believe in myself.
She talked about herself.

grammar.explanation: 아직 means "still" or, with a negative, "not yet", for something that has not changed or finished up to now. 여전히 means "still, as before", stressing that a situation remains the same as it was.

examples.en: My friend hasn’t come yet.
I am still doing my homework.
He is still busy (as always).

grammar.explanation: Some adverbs only work in negative sentences. 별로 softens a negative to "not very / not really", while 전혀 makes it absolute, "not at all". Use them with 안, ~지 않다, 못 or 없다/모르다.

examples.en: I’m not very hungry.
That movie wasn’t really fun.
I don’t eat meat at all.
I don’t know that person at all.

grammar.explanation: 훨씬 goes in front of a descriptive word in a comparison with ~보다 to say "much more" or "far". It intensifies the gap between the two things being compared.

examples.en: Today is much colder than yesterday.
The train is much faster than the bus.
Korean is much harder than English.

grammar.explanation: Use N에 관한 + noun or N에 관해(서) + verb to mean "about / regarding" a topic. 관련하다 has a similar meaning and is very common as 관련된 ("related to") in front of a noun.

examples.en: I read a book about Korean history.
We talked about this problem.

examples.ko: 저는 환경과 관련된 일을 하고 싶어요.
examples.en: I want to do work related to the environment.

grammar.explanation: 주위 refers to the area surrounding something or someone. Put it after a noun (N 주위에) for "around N", or use 주위 사람 for the people around you.

examples.en: There are many trees around the house.
The people around me are all kind.
He looked around his surroundings.

grammar.explanation: 일단 marks the action you will do first before anything else, often followed by ~고 or ~(으)ㄴ 후에. It can also mean "for now" when deciding on a temporary step.

examples.en: First I will eat, and then study.

examples.ko: 일단 숙제를 끝낸 후에 친구를 만날 거예요.
examples.en: Once I finish my homework, I will meet a friend.
Let’s go home for now.

grammar.point: Weight words: 무게, 몸무게, 살이 찌다/빠지다
grammar.explanation: 무게 is the weight of an object and 몸무게 is a person’s body weight. To talk about gaining or losing weight, use 살 (flesh) as the subject: 살이 찌다 is to gain weight and 살이 빠지다 is to lose it.

examples.en: I gained a lot of weight lately.
I exercised, so I lost weight.
How much does this bag weigh?

lessons.title: Lesson 35: It seems to be/might be: 것 같다

vocab.en: to be unfolded, to be unrolled
to be stuffy, to be frustrated
to be amazing, to be cool

grammar.explanation: Take the future modifier ~(으)ㄹ 것 and put 같다 after it to make a guess: "I think it will" or "it is likely to". It works with verbs and adjectives, and 같아요 is often pronounced 같애요 in speech.

examples.en: I think it will rain tomorrow.
This movie will probably be fun.
My junior is probably going to be late.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 새우를 안 먹을 것 같아요.
examples.en: I don’t think that person will eat shrimp.

grammar.explanation: Change the modifier before 것 같다 to talk about the present or past: ~는 for present actions, ~(으)ㄴ for past actions or present-tense adjectives. These forms suggest you are judging from some evidence, while ~았/었을 것 같다 is more of a blind guess about the past.

examples.en: It seems to be raining outside.

examples.ko: 친구가 벌써 집에 간 것 같아요.
examples.en: It seems my friend already went home.

examples.ko: 이 수영장은 아주 깊은 것 같아요.
examples.en: This pool seems very deep.

examples.ko: 아빠가 벌써 돈을 냈을 것 같아요.
examples.en: Dad has probably already paid.

grammar.explanation: 그렇다 combined with 것 같다 gives handy replies: 그런 것 같아요 ("it seems so / I think so") and 그럴 것 같아요 ("it will probably be so"). Negate with 그렇지 않은 것 같아요.

examples.en: Yes, I think so.
It will probably be like that.
No, I don’t think so.

grammar.explanation: Adding ~겠 to a stem can express a guess or impression based on what you see or hear, like "it must be" or "it looks like it will". It is common in reactions to someone else’s situation.

examples.en: Wow, this honey must be really delicious!
You worked all day, so you must be tired.
That fishing trip sounds like it will be really fun.

lessons.title: Lesson 36: To look like: 보이다 / ~아/어 보이다

vocab.en: to move to a new house
to gain, to get, to obtain

grammar.point: N 같이 보이다 (to look like N)
grammar.explanation: 보이다 means "to be seen", so it is often translated as "can see". Put a noun before 같이 and end with 보이다 to say that something looks like that noun.

examples.en: You look like a teacher.
That cloud looks like a fox.
That man looks like a celebrity.

grammar.explanation: 보이다 and 들리다 are passive-like verbs meaning "to be seen" and "to be heard". The thing seen or heard takes ~이/가, and English usually translates them as "I can see / I can hear".

examples.en: I can’t see the mountain from here.
Can you see the fire station?
I can’t hear your voice well.
I heard a strange sound outside.

grammar.point: N 맛 같다 / N 냄새 같다 (tastes/smells like)
grammar.explanation: 맛 means taste and 냄새 means smell. Put the noun being compared before 맛 or 냄새 and follow it with 같다 to say something tastes or smells like it.

examples.en: This food tastes like kimchi.
This candy tastes like strawberry.
This perfume smells like roses.

grammar.explanation: Attach ~아/어 보이다 to an adjective stem to say how something appears: "looks tired", "looks salty". The ending 보이다 then takes the tense and politeness.

examples.en: You look tired today.
That food looks salty.
This studio looks very nice.
My younger sibling looked happy.

grammar.explanation: Attach ~아/어서 to a verb or adjective stem to make the first clause the reason for the second. It is very common in speech, but the second clause cannot be a command or a suggestion.

examples.en: I was hungry, so I ate my lunch box.
The road was jammed, so I was late.
I was so excited that I couldn’t sleep.

grammar.explanation: Past or future markers are never put before ~아/어서. The tense of the whole sentence is shown only on the final verb, so the reason clause takes its time from it.

examples.en: It rained yesterday, so I stayed home.
I’ll be busy tomorrow, so I won’t be able to go.
I forgot my homework, so the teacher got angry.

grammar.explanation: With 이다, the reason form is usually (이)라서: 이라서 after a consonant, 라서 after a vowel. The negative is 아니라서, "because it is not N".

examples.en: It’s a long holiday, so the highway is jammed.
I’m a student, so I don’t have much money.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 스님이라서 고기를 안 먹어요.
examples.en: He is a monk, so he doesn’t eat meat.
It’s not the latest phone, so it’s slow.

grammar.explanation: 그래서 starts a new sentence and links it to the previous one as its result, much like "so" or "therefore". It is the sentence-starting version of ~아/어서.

examples.ko: 어제 너무 피곤했어요. 그래서 일찍 잤어요.
examples.en: I was very tired yesterday. So I went to bed early.

examples.ko: 비가 많이 왔어요. 그래서 집에 있었어요.
examples.en: It rained a lot. So I stayed home.

examples.ko: 도시락을 깜빡했어요. 그래서 점심을 못 먹었어요.
examples.en: I forgot my lunch box. So I couldn’t eat lunch.

grammar.explanation: 때문 is a noun meaning "reason". Place it right after a noun with ~에 to say "because of" that noun.

examples.en: I couldn’t go on the trip because of the rain.
I was late because of you.
I’m busy these days because of exams.

grammar.explanation: Add ~기 때문에 to a verb or adjective stem to give a reason; it sounds a little firmer and more formal than ~아/어서. Like ~아/어서, the following clause should not be a command or suggestion.

examples.en: I can’t meet today because I’m busy.

examples.ko: 거리가 북적거리기 때문에 집에 있을 거예요.
examples.en: I’ll stay home because the streets are crowded.
He wears a school uniform because he is a student.

grammar.explanation: Unlike ~아/어서, ~기 때문에 can carry its own tense. Use ~았/었기 때문에 for a past reason and ~(으)ㄹ 것이기 때문에 for a future one.

examples.en: I made money because I invested in stocks.
I’m tired because I went to bed late yesterday.

examples.ko: 내일 비가 올 것이기 때문에 우산을 가져갈 거예요.
examples.en: I will take an umbrella because it will rain tomorrow.

grammar.explanation: End a sentence with ~기 때문이에요 to state "it is because ...", often after 이유는 ("the reason is") or 왜냐하면. 그렇기 때문에 at the start of a sentence means "because of that / therefore".

examples.ko: 제가 늦은 이유는 길이 막혔기 때문이에요.
examples.en: The reason I was late is that the road was jammed.
Because I’m too tired.

examples.ko: 비가 많이 와요. 그렇기 때문에 밖에 안 나갈 거예요.
examples.en: It’s raining a lot. Therefore, I won’t go out.

vocab.en: to spoil, to ruin, to screw up

grammar.explanation: Add ~시 (after a vowel) or ~으시 (after a consonant) to a stem when the person doing the action deserves respect, no matter who you are talking to. Stems ending in ㄹ drop the ㄹ (살다 → 사시다), and the result is then conjugated normally, e.g. 가세요, 가셨어요.

examples.en: Grandfather is reading the newspaper.
The teacher came to school yesterday.
Grandmother lives in Seoul.
Father cooked in the kitchen.

grammar.explanation: Some verbs have their own honorific forms instead of just adding ~시. 드시다 or 잡수시다 replace 먹다, 주무시다 replaces 자다, and 계시다 replaces 있다 when it means being in a place.

examples.en: Grandmother is sleeping now.
Father is at home.
Grandfather ate dinner.
Good night.

grammar.point: 드리다 and ~께 (to give to someone respected)
grammar.explanation: When the receiver deserves respect, use 드리다 instead of 주다, and the particle ~께 instead of ~에게/한테. 드리다 also replaces 주다 when doing something for a respected person.

examples.en: I gave Grandfather a present.
I will give the teacher a letter.
I want to give my parents flowers.

grammar.explanation: 말씀하다 (usually 말씀하시다) is the respectful way to say that a respected person speaks. The noun 말씀 is used for a respected person’s words, and also humbly for your own words to them, as in 말씀을 드리다.

examples.en: The professor spoke slowly.
I listened carefully to the teacher’s words.
I told Grandmother.

grammar.explanation: The simplest command is just the present-tense conjugation of a verb, said as an order; the subject is usually dropped. Without 요 it is for friends or younger people, and adding 요 makes it polite.

examples.en: Come quickly!
Sit here.
Go straight at the next intersection.
Eat this.

grammar.explanation: ~(으)세요 is ~(으)시 plus ~어요, making a polite and respectful request or instruction. It is the most common way to tell someone to do something in everyday polite speech.

examples.en: Please sit here.
Goodbye (go well).

examples.ko: 이 약을 하루에 세 번 드세요.
examples.en: Take this medicine three times a day.
Please go to the right.

grammar.explanation: ~아/어라 is a blunt, plain-style command used to people younger or lower in status, such as parents to children, or in written instructions. It sounds strong, so avoid it with superiors.

examples.en: Get up quickly!
Do your homework first.
Stay still.
Eat a lot.

grammar.explanation: ~(으)십시오 is the most formal command, heard in announcements, signs, and from staff to customers. It shows high respect to the listener.

examples.en: Please be seated here.
Please come inside.
Please wait a moment.
Goodbye (go well).

grammar.explanation: To tell someone not to do something, attach ~지 말다 to the verb stem and put the imperative ending on 말다: ~지 마, ~지 마세요, ~지 마라, ~지 마십시오.

examples.en: Please don’t smoke here.
Don’t worry.
Do not touch that object.
Don’t be late.

grammar.explanation: To ask someone to give you something, put an imperative ending on 주다: 줘, 주세요, 주십시오. Adding 좀 softens the request and makes it sound more polite.

examples.en: Please give me some water.
Give me that book.
Two apples, please.

grammar.explanation: Attach ~아/어 주다 to a verb stem to show the action is done as a favor or benefit for someone. With an imperative ending (~아/어 주세요) it becomes a polite "please do ... for me", and 보여 주다 means "to show".

examples.en: Mom made a lunch box for me.
My colleague helped me with my work.
Please open the window.
Please show me that picture.

grammar.explanation: Combine ~지 말다 with ~아/어 주다 to ask someone not to do something as a favor: ~지 말아 주세요. It is softer than a plain ~지 마세요.

examples.en: Please don’t make noise here.
Please don’t come into my room.
Please don’t be late tomorrow.

grammar.explanation: To thank someone for doing something, add ~아/어 주다 to the verb, then ~아/어서 ("because"), then 고맙다 or 감사하다. With respected people, use ~아/어 주셔서 감사합니다.

examples.en: Thank you for coming.
Thank you for helping me.
Thanks for listening to me.
Thank you for cooking dinner.

vocab.en: to cheer on, to root for
at any rate, in any case, anyways

grammar.point: Noun + 때 (at the time of N)
grammar.explanation: 때 means "time". Put it after a noun for an event or period, like 방학 때 or 점심 때, to mean "during / at that time". 그때 means "at that time".

examples.en: I will go to Korea during vacation.
I ate my lunch box at lunchtime.
At that time, I was a student.

grammar.explanation: Attach ~(으)ㄹ 때 to a verb or adjective stem to describe the moment when something happens; the main clause happens during that time, not after it. It can refer to the future or to a general habit, and ~에 after 때 is usually dropped.

examples.en: I listen to music when I study.

examples.ko: 밥을 먹을 때 텔레비전을 보지 마세요.
examples.en: Don’t watch TV while you eat.
I drink coffee when I’m tired.
I sing when I wash my hair.

grammar.explanation: For a time in the past, put ~았/었 before ~을 때. 어렸을 때 ("when I was young") is a common way to talk about childhood.

examples.ko: 한국에 있었을 때 한국어를 많이 배웠어요.
examples.en: I learned a lot of Korean when I was in Korea.
When I was young, I was scared of insects.
When I arrived home, nobody was there.

grammar.explanation: Other particles can follow 때: 때까지 ("until"), 때부터 ("since"), 때마다 ("every time") and 때는 (contrast or topic).

examples.en: I have liked soccer since I was young.
Every time I hear that song, I’m happy.
When it rains, I stay home.
I will wait until my friend comes.
